Britain and Spain had been urged in 1964 to start talks on the colony's future, and past votes in 1965 and 1966 had kept the push alive. Laura Díaz-Martínez, Juan Giménez-Abián, Yoshiaki Azuma, and co-authors pinned down a protein that human cells need to divide correctly, in a 2006 study. When a cell splits, its chromosomes must be shared faithfully between the two daughters. Errors in that segregation cause the chromosome chaos seen in many cancers.

The protein PIAS-gamma proved required for faithful chromosome segregation in human cells. Without it, the sharing goes wrong. Identifying required parts of the division machinery is basic work with long reach: each such protein is a possible marker of unstable cancers and a possible target. instrument-of-government-1653:
England gained its first written constitution in December 1653, when the Council of Officers adopted the Instrument of Government. John Lambert did much of the drafting. The plan replaced the Rump Parliament after the Civil War and named Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector, the country's single head of state.

Power was split three ways: the Protector ruled with a Council of State, and a Parliament chosen every three years held the purse and made laws. The text also promised freedom of worship to most Protestants and set rules for votes and seats. It worked for less than four years, yet later constitution writers still study its design.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d53: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on October 22, 1943, the day after their previous exchange in this series. The letter is Document 53 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d153: On November 21, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and two more Churchill notes of the same date follow in the volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d253:
President Roosevelt's morning calls at Cairo on 23 November 1943 are reconstructed by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The Log lists the visitors: Vyshinsky, Mountbatten, Churchill with his daughter, the Chiangs, and three Chinese generals. No memoranda of the talks were made, so the editors rely on letters from Harriman and Bohlen.

The fullest account concerns Andrey Vyshinsky, who was passing through on his way to serve as the Soviet member of the Advisory Council for Italy. Roosevelt urged close three-power cooperation on that council, aired his troubles with de Gaulle, and floated trusteeship for immature countries, naming Morocco. Vyshinsky agreed in general terms and seemed struck by the President's frankness. The note also weighs when Tehran lodging invitations from Russia and Britain reached Roosevelt.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d353:
The Log of the President's trip continues with the Tehran chapter, covering 27 November to 2 December 1943. Kept hour by hour by Lieutenant William Rigdon, it opens with a fog-delayed departure from Cairo on the morning of 27 November.

The President's plane took off at seven minutes past seven. It flew 1,310 miles in about six and a half hours. The route passed over the Suez Canal and circled Jerusalem for the view. It then followed the Lend-Lease road and rail lines across Iraq and Iran. Trainloads of supplies bound for Russia could be seen from the air. The party landed at Gale Morghe airport, a Russian army field south of Tehran, with no honors, by request, for security. General Connolly met the President, who drove straight to the American Legation.

President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on February 23, 1944, keeping up the direct correspondence the two men had begun before they ever met. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, in its follow-up section.

By February the Red Army was advancing fast, and the questions between Washington and Moscow mixed military coordination with the first hard problems of Poland and the postwar map. Roosevelt's letters to Stalin worked to hold the partnership steady through those strains. For readers, this message belongs to the testing season of the alliance, when Tehran's goodwill met the realities of armies moving west.
frus-1944-quebec-d53:
Lester B. Pearson, Canada's ambassador in Washington, wrote to Harry Hopkins on September 3, 1944. Pearson, later Canada's prime minister, was then his country's chief envoy to the United States. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Canada was host to the coming conference and a full partner in the war, and Pearson's channel to Hopkins handled the Canadian side of the arrangements from Washington. A message in this channel shows the host country working quietly inside the alliance's machinery. For readers, it adds a diplomat of future fame to the conference's supporting cast.
frus-1944-quebec-d153:
British strategy for the war against Japan is set out in this chiefs of staff memorandum of August 23, 1944. Since the Sextant Conference, American forces had raced across the Pacific, Japan had reinforced Burma to ten divisions, and Germany's possible collapse might soon free troops. London had studied how British forces could best help finish the Pacific war.

The paper rejects continuing the slog in North Burma, where sickness alone cost 282,000 casualties in early 1944. Instead it backs Mountbatten's Vanguard plan: seize Rangoon by airborne assault and cut Japan's communications in Burma. It also offers a strong British fleet, built around new battleships and carriers, to serve under American command in the main operations against Japan by mid-1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d253:
Roosevelt answered Stettinius from Quebec on September 15, 1944, and the compromise voting formula found no favor. Neither he nor Churchill was inclined to approve the proposed amendment. Roosevelt's own thought was to record the subject in the Dumbarton Oaks agreement as discussed but undecided, leaving it to the meeting of the United Nations.

Churchill feared that course would be unacceptable to the Russians. They would know they faced overwhelming defeat in a United Nations meeting, grow sore, and take it out on the allies on some other point. Roosevelt counseled keeping on trying. Failing agreement, he preferred silence about the disagreement, or a general statement that certain points remained open. The editors note both London and Moscow soon rejected the formula officially.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d53: Roosevelt closed this opening run of papers with a message to Churchill on 12 January 1945. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d153:
From Warm Springs on 15 December 1944, Roosevelt asked Churchill what to do next about Poland. His top secret telegram, number 674, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the prime minister's Commons statement on the Polish question.

Roosevelt wants Churchill's judgment on two things. First, can Mikolajczyk come back into power with enough authority to carry out his plans? Second, what should the allies do if the Lublin Committee declares itself Poland's provisional government and Stalin recognizes it? He wonders whether to ask Stalin to hold off any firm step until the three leaders meet. Pressure at home, he adds, may force him to publish the policy points of his letter to Mikolajczyk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d253:
Stalin argued for an invasion through Switzerland at a Moscow military conference, Harriman reported on 15 October 1944. His account to the President, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, covers the previous night's session. General Brooke, backed by Churchill, had laid out the allied plans.

Stalin called the attack on the Ruhr the knockout blow for Germany, yet again urged turning the Siegfried Line from the south, through Switzerland. Churchill explained why that move would not work, and voiced confidence in the drive in the north. On Italy, Stalin showed keen interest in landings on the Istrian peninsula, and in allied and Soviet forces joining hands in Austria. General Antonov then gave the Red Army's position, starting with an offensive in the far north, two miles from Petsamo.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d353:
Alger Hiss filled pages with pencil notes during the February 6, 1945 plenary at Livadia Palace. His jottings open with errands — a note to the President, pictures to be sent, a redraft on voting — then list who sat where. Creation, prophecy, providence, and the divine attributes all receive long, careful analysis, including his famous teaching that God is best described by what God is not. The Guide became the major work of medieval Jewish thought and influenced Christian and Muslim philosophy as well. It rewards slow reading and punishes skimming.
tob-4053:
E. A. Wallis Budge's translation of the Book of the Dead rests on the Papyrus of Ani, the most complete surviving copy of the Egyptian funerary text. Ani was a royal scribe, and his scroll follows his passage through the underworld step by step, illustrated vignette by vignette. The famous judgment scene, heart weighed against the feather of truth, comes from this very manuscript.

Spells, hymns, and confessions accompany the pictures, giving readers the text as one Egyptian actually owned it rather than as a composite. Budge's edition made Ani's papyrus world famous. For ancient Egypt's afterlife in its finest surviving manuscript, no other single scroll compares.
tob-0153:
Crowley launched The Equinox in 1909 as a review of scientific illuminism, part journal, part manifesto for his new magical order. Volume one, number one opens the series. Manifestos, rituals, and the first statements of his system fill its large pages.

Poems, essays, and book reviews stand beside formal instruction, since Crowley meant the review to shape taste as well as practice. The production was lavish for an occult journal. This entry draws on a verified pre-1930 edition. Later numbers grew more notorious, but the program of the whole venture is set here: magic presented as a public, printed discipline.
tob-4153:
Eliphas Levi's Transcendental Magic, first published in French in the 1850s, effectively invented modern occultism. Waite's 1896 English translation divides the work into doctrine and ritual. Levi names the astral light as the great agent behind magic, and links the tarot, the pentagram, and Kabbalah into one system.

His pages swagger with confidence, mixing real learning with grand showmanship. Every magician since, from the Golden Dawn to Crowley, stands in Levi's debt or in his shadow. Verified from the 1919 edition, Waite's version remains the standard English Levi. Few occult books have been so often quoted, or so seldom read whole.
tob-4253:
Thomas M. N. Owen collected Southern folk-magic tales in Old Rabbit, the Voodoo, and Other Sorcerers, published in 1893. Br'er Rabbit's trickster kin, conjure workers, and root doctors move through his dialect stories. Owen wrote down what he heard from Black storytellers of the South, in their narrative manner.

Spells, haunts, and cunning escapes fill the pages, along with humor that cuts as deep as the fear. The collection preserves a living tradition of conjure and tale-telling that print was already changing. Verified from the 1919 edition, Owen's volume remains a vivid early record of Southern folk magic in story form.
tob-13153:
Manly P. Hall wrote The Lost Keys of Freemasonry in 1923, when he was twenty-two, years before his fame as an occult lecturer. The short book reads Masonry as a spiritual teaching hidden in symbols. It became a beloved primer inside and outside the lodges.

Hall treats the lodge, the degrees, and the lost word of the master mason as signs of man's search for light and truth. The true lost key, he argues, is within the Mason himself. Masons have handed the book to new members for a century, and it shows the symbolic reading of the craft at its most earnest.
robertson-panel-report-1953:
In January 1953, a panel of scientists met for the CIA to judge the flood of UFO reports. Chaired by physicist H. P. Robertson, it produced the report later called the Durant Report. The file here includes the main report and its three added tabs.

The panel found no proof of craft from other worlds and no direct threat. But it feared mass reports could clog defense channels in a crisis. It urged a public teaching campaign to calm sightings, and quiet watch on civilian saucer groups. The plan shaped official UFO policy for years.
lepsius-letters-egypt-ethiopia-sinai-185:
Richard Lepsius wrote home from the first true survey of Egypt in his Letters, set in English in 1853. Lepsius led a band sent by the king of Prussia in 1842. They drew, gauged, and logged shrines from the Nile's mouth to deep Nubia and the hills of Sinai with a care no trek had matched.

Each note mixes trek life with hard fact. New kings, dates, and scripts fall into place as he works. The notes are a log of a field at its birth. Their zest and grit still pull fans in.
whewell-plurality-worlds-1853:
William Whewell was a master of many fields at Cambridge. In 1853 he put out a bold tract with no name on it. The tract argues that Earth may stand alone as a home of life. It struck at the claim of a host of lived-in worlds.

Whewell weighs heat, light, and the size of each planet. He holds that most worlds are too hot, too cold, or too wild for life. The tract drew a sharp reply from David Brewster. The clash set off ten years of print debate on the worlds.
dickens-bleak-house-1853:
Charles Dickens published Bleak House in 1853, his great novel of the Court of Chancery. The suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce drags on for years and ruins all it touches. Dickens aimed at a legal system that fed on delay, cost, and human hope.

Esther Summerson tells half the tale, and a grave narrator tells the rest. Lady Dedlock hides a secret that a cold lawyer hunts through fog and law. A crossing sweeper, Jo, spreads disease and shows how all ranks link in London. The suit ends when costs eat the whole estate it fought over for years. Fog, law, and charity give the book its vast and sombre power.
bronte-villette-1853:
Charlotte Brontë published Villette in 1853, her most psychologically intricate novel of inner life. The book is a landmark of interior narrative and unconsummated desire in Victorian fiction and beyond. It draws on her own years as a teacher in Brussels, thinly masked as Villette.

Lucy Snowe, penniless and alone, teaches English at a girls' school in a foreign town. She watches, hides, and endures while others court, quarrel, and shine around her quiet post there. The fiery Paul Emanuel slowly sees her worth, and a storm clouds their parting at sea. A spectral nun, a drugged night fête, and confessions to a priest crowd Lucy's path. Brontë leaves the end veiled, and readers still argue Lucy's fate with real heat.
dumas-countess-of-charny-1853:
Alexandre Dumas published The Countess of Charny in 1853, climax of his Marie Antoinette romances in French. Henry Llewellyn Williams made this English version of the Revolution's climax and Louis XVI's end. The vast serial brought Dumas's revolutionary cycle to its scaffold close in Paris at last.

Andrée, now Countess of Charny, and Gilbert move through the monarchy's fall and the Terror's rise. The royal family's flight to Varennes, the Temple prison, and the king's trial fill these pages. Old friends from the earlier romances meet fates of exile, madness, and the guillotine in Paris. Dumas pauses for long views of the crowd, the court, and the Revolution's driving ideas in France. The cycle ends in elegy for a world the Revolution swept wholly away.
hawthorne-tanglewood-tales-1853:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Tanglewood Tales in 1853, his second volume of Greek myths for children. With A Wonder-Book, it forms the canon of children's classical mythology in English for the young. Eustace Bright returns to Tanglewood with six more tales for his troop of child listeners there.

Theseus threads the labyrinth, Jason seeks the Golden Fleece, and Circe turns men to swine. Hawthorne keeps the marvels and trims the blood, though his Ulysses still outwits monsters and storms. The children interrupt, doubt, and delight, giving the old myths a living fireside air in Massachusetts. His prose makes Greek names feel like household words to readers meeting them for the first time. Generations met the classical world first in these two friendly, golden volumes of tales.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-2-1853:
John Ruskin continued The Stones of Venice with Volume 2 in 1853, subtitled The Sea-Stories. This volume reads Venetian history through the city's churches and palaces. The Byzantine and Gothic periods receive the richest treatment. St. Mark's and the Doge's Palace stand as lessons in stone.

Ruskin links each style to the faith and freedom of its age. Gothic, for him, joins nature, variety, and the worker's liberty. The famous chapter on the nature of Gothic influenced William Morris and the labor movement. The volume is the core of Ruskin's moral aesthetics. It teaches readers to see buildings as history made visible.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-3-1853:
John Ruskin completed The Stones of Venice with Volume 3 in 1853, subtitled The Fall. The volume turns to the Renaissance and the decline of Venice. Ruskin blames pride, luxury, and cold classical rules for the decay of Venetian art. Churches and tombs of the later period show, to his eye, skill without soul.

He ends with warnings to England, which he feared was following Venice's path. The argument is severe, yet the descriptions of light, water, and stone are glorious. The three volumes together form a parable of rise and fall. They changed how Britain thought about architecture. The work remains Ruskin's masterpiece.
comte-positive-philosophy-martineau-1853:
Auguste Comte's main work reached English readers in 1853, in Harriet Martineau's short version. Comte, a French thinker, held that sound knowledge rests on facts we can observe. His law of three stages says thought moves from gods to abstract ideas to tested science. Volume 1 covers numbers, the stars, and the study of matter in that scheme.

Martineau cut Comte's six French volumes down to two English ones, with his blessing. Her clear text carried his ideas across the English-speaking world. Comte also ranks the fields of study from the most simple to the most complex. His new science of society crowns the scheme in the next volume.
maurice-theological-essays-1853:
Frederick Denison Maurice was a Broad Church theologian and a founder of Christian socialism in England. His Theological Essays, published in 1853, cost him his professorship at King's College London. The essays serve as the Broad Church manifesto and liberal Anglican theology's charter.

Maurice challenges narrow readings of atonement, eternal punishment, and the Bible that had hardened into tests of loyalty. His essay on eternal life and eternal death, read as denying endless torment, brought the storm that ended his post. Maurice accepted the loss calmly, and his influence on the church's social conscience only grew.
ramesey-astrologia-restaurata-1653:
William Ramesey was a physician and astrologer under the Commonwealth whose Astrologia Restaurata appeared in 1653. The title promises astrology restored, purged of error and set in order. Ramesey served great households and wrote for students of the art alike.

He rebuilds the system from Ptolemy and the Arab masters, covering nativities, elections, and the weather in one scheme. His pages mix medical practice with star lore, since his patients expected both from the same man. The book preserves the Commonwealth astrologer's full system at the height of the art's English power. He writes with the confidence of a man whose art still had patrons.
galileo-sidereus-nuncius-1653:
Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius, The Starry Messenger, appears here in the 1653 London Latin printing. Galileo published the work in Latin in 1610, reporting what his improved telescope showed. No public-domain English translation exists for this line, so the text stands in Latin, as early readers across Europe read it.

Galileo reported mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter, and crowds of stars inside the Milky Way. Each sight struck the old picture of perfect, unchanging heavens. News of the book raced across Europe and made Galileo famous and suspect at once. The slim 1610 report, kept here in its 1653 London form, is one of the founding documents of modern astronomy.
linnaeus-species-plantarum-vol1-1753:
Carl Linnaeus published Species Plantarum, Volume 1, in 1753. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. Botanists count 1753 and this book as the starting point of botanical nomenclature, the fixed year from which plant names are judged.

Volume 1 lists the plant species Linnaeus knew, each with a short diagnostic phrase and a one-word trivial name in the margin. Those marginal names became the second half of each plant's two-part scientific name. Linnaeus drew on gardens, herbaria, and reports from his traveling students worldwide. The volume is slim beside its influence: every plant name in science traces its standing, in part, to these pages.
linnaeus-species-plantarum-vol2-1753:
Volume 2 of Linnaeus's Species Plantarum appeared in 1753, completing the work in the same year it began. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. Together the two volumes named and described the plant world as one Swedish professor and his network knew it.

The second volume carries the species list through the remaining classes of his sexual system, with habitats and synonyms from older writers. Linnaeus meant the pair as a complete inventory, a flora of the whole world in brief entries. Later botanists corrected and expanded it beyond measure. Yet the 1753 pair still stands as the completion of the botanical system and the baseline of plant naming.
cornelius-nepos-lives-watson-1853:
Cornelius Nepos, a friend of Cicero, wrote short lives of great commanders around 40 BCE, the first such book in Latin. The men are mostly Greeks and Carthaginians, not Romans. The Reverend John Selby Watson translated the lives into English in 1853, with a notice on the life of Nepos himself.

Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristides, and Epaminondas stand beside Hannibal, Cato, and Atticus, each life told in a few plain pages. Nepos cared more for character and fair judgment than for long war reports. His little book set the pattern for biography in the Roman world and was read in schools for centuries after.
eutropius-abridgment-watson-1853:
Eutropius wrote his Breviarium, a short history of Rome, around 369 CE for the emperor Valens, who wanted the past in brief. John Selby Watson translated it into English in 1853, adding a notice on the author's life. In ten slim books the story runs from Romulus to the emperor Jovian.

Each reign gets a few crisp lines: wars won, lands gained, emperors made and unmade. The plain style made the book a school text for a thousand years, the most copied Roman history of the Middle Ages. Readers who want the whole arc of Rome in one short read still start here.
justin-epitome-trogus-watson-1853:
Trogus Pompeius, a Gaul who wrote in Latin under Augustus, composed a forty-four-book history of the world outside Rome. His work is lost, but Justin cut it down into an epitome some time in the second to fourth century CE. John Selby Watson translated Justin into English in 1853, with a notice on Trogus.

Justin keeps the rise and fall of Assyria, Persia, and the kingdoms that split the empire of Alexander. Parthia gets a full, rare account, and early Rome appears in brief. For the Hellenistic east, Justin is often the only thread that survives. His short books guided readers to Trogus for over a thousand years.
henry-huntingdon-chronicle-forester-1853:
Henry, archdeacon of Huntingdon, wrote his Historia Anglorum at the order of his bishop, and carried it to the year 1154. Thomas Forester translated the chronicle into English in 1853. Henry tells the story of England from the Roman landing to the death of King Stephen.

He frames the tale as five great plagues of invasion sent for the sins of the land. They are the Romans, the Picts and Scots, the Saxons, the Danes, and the Normans. Battle pieces, speeches, and verses of his own stud the prose. Henry knew the court of Henry I and wrote of men his elders had seen. His chronicle is a key voice of the twelfth century.
william-newburgh-history-stevenson-1853:
William of Newburgh, an Augustinian canon in Yorkshire, wrote his History of English Affairs in the 1190s. It covers the years from the Norman Conquest to 1198. Joseph Stevenson translated the work in 1853. William is often called the most critical of the English historians of the twelfth century, and he earns the praise.

He weighs his sources, mocks Geoffrey of Monmouth's tales of Arthur as lies, and tells even wonders with a raised brow. The reigns of Stephen, Henry II, and Richard pass under his cool judgment. His tale of the civil war of Stephen's time is a chief source for the anarchy. Northern voices are rare in this age, and his is the best.
postel-de-originibus-1553:
Guillaume Postel, the wandering French scholar, published De Originibus at Basel in 1553, with the printer Oporinus. The text is in Latin. Postel had traveled the Ottoman world, learned Arabic, Hebrew, and more, and come home preaching the concord of all peoples under one faith. His book treats the origins of languages, letters, and nations after the flood.

He derives the peoples of the earth from the sons of Noah and argues that Hebrew stands at the root of the tongues. Christian Kabbalah, Greek myth, and travelers' reports blend in his pages. Postel's dream of world concord made him famous and got him locked up as a madman and a heretic. The book is his map of that dream.
guicciardini-history-of-italy-goddard-vo:
Francesco Guicciardini, a Florentine statesman, wrote his Storia d'Italia between 1537 and 1540, and it was first printed in 1561. Volume one here opens Austin Parke Goddard's English translation, issued from 1753 to 1761 in ten volumes. Guicciardini had served popes and governed cities, and he wrote Italy's recent past as an insider.

His subject is the Italian wars, the long invasion and struggle that began in 1494. France, Spain, and the empire fought across a peninsula split into rival states. Guicciardini traces how that split invited ruin, with a cool, probing mind. His work is often called the first modern analytical history, and volume one shows why.

Volume two continues Goddard's English version of Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy, the translation of 1753 to 1761. Guicciardini wrote the Storia d'Italia in 1537 to 1540, after a career at the top of Florentine and papal politics. It reached print in 1561, after his death, and Europe read it as a revelation.

The history follows the Italian wars year by year, siege by siege, treaty by broken treaty. Guicciardini refuses simple blame: ambition, fear, and chance share the guilt in his pages. His divided Italy stands as a warning of what disunion costs a rich land. Volume two keeps his clear, severe analysis moving through the storm.

Goddard's translation of Guicciardini's History of Italy reaches volume three of ten. Francesco Guicciardini composed the work between 1537 and 1540, drawing on state papers and his own years in high office. The Storia d'Italia was first printed in 1561 and soon ranked with the great histories of the age.

Its theme is tragedy at national scale: a brilliant, wealthy peninsula torn by its own rivalries. Foreign kings marched in, and Italian states called them in against each other. Guicciardini weighs each prince and republic with the same unsparing hand. Later historians learned from his method of close, causal analysis. Volume three carries that method deeper into the wars.

Volume four of Goddard's English Guicciardini, from the ten-volume translation of 1753 to 1761, continues the History of Italy. Francesco Guicciardini wrote the original in 1537 to 1540, and it was printed in 1561. He had governed Modena and the Romagna for the pope, and negotiated with kings, before turning to history in forced retirement.

Retirement gave him distance, and distance gave the book its cool, dissecting power. The Italian wars unfold in his pages as a chain of choices, each one narrowing the next. No hero escapes his scrutiny, and no folly lacks its cause. Volume four holds the middle of that chain, link by hard link.

Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy reaches its fifth volume in Goddard's translation, the English set of 1753 to 1761. The Italian work, written in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561, covers the decades when Italy became the battleground of Europe. Guicciardini knew the courts he describes from the inside.

At the midpoint of the set, his great argument stands fully visible. Italy's states, rich and cultured, lacked union, and so fell prey to France, Spain, and the empire in turn. Guicciardini tells the story with a statesman's grasp of motive and money. His history founded a cooler, modern way of explaining events. Volume five keeps that explanation at full strength.

Volume six continues Goddard's ten-volume English Guicciardini, translated between 1753 and 1761. Francesco Guicciardini's Storia d'Italia, written in 1537 to 1540 and first printed in 1561, narrates the Italian wars from 1494 onward. The author had served as ambassador to Spain and as a papal governor, and his history breathes that experience.

Campaigns, leagues, and betrayals fill these pages, each traced to the interests that drove it. Guicciardini trusted no slogan and no hero, only the record and the motive behind it. That habit made his book the first truly analytical history of the modern kind. Volume six advances the long tragedy of a divided peninsula, told by one of its ablest sons.

Goddard's English History of Italy by Francesco Guicciardini moves into volume seven of ten. The translation ran from 1753 to 1761; the Italian original was written in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561. Guicciardini, once a power in Florence and the papal states, wrote the wars of his age as a man who had helped to wage them.

The seventh volume keeps his steady gaze on the struggle for Italy. Great powers clash, small states scheme, and the peninsula pays for every bargain. Guicciardini's genius lies in showing how each disaster grew from choices men praised at the time. His cool method still teaches historians how to argue from evidence. The tragedy deepens here.

Volume eight of Goddard's translation continues Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy toward its later books. The English set ran to ten volumes between 1753 and 1761. Guicciardini's Italian text, composed in 1537 to 1540 and printed in 1561, had long been a classic before Goddard Englished it.

The wars roll on in these pages: France and the empire fighting over Italian soil, Italian states shifting sides to survive. Guicciardini anatomizes each shift with a surgeon's patience. He shows a peninsula whose disunion turned its wealth into a prize for others. Readers rank the work as the first modern analytical history for good reason. Volume eight sustains that rank, campaign by campaign.

The ninth volume of Goddard's English Guicciardini stands one step from the end of the ten-volume set. Francesco Guicciardini wrote his History of Italy in 1537 to 1540; it was printed in 1561, after his death. Goddard's translation, 1753 to 1761, brought the Florentine's masterpiece to English readers entire.

Near the close, the Italian wars have consumed a generation, and Guicciardini's verdict has only hardened. Division invited invasion; invasion fed on division; and Italy's states learned too late. His analysis stays close to councils, purses, and armies, where causes truly live. Volume nine carries the great history to the edge of its somber end, with its method undimmed.

Volume ten completes Goddard's English translation of Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy, the set of 1753 to 1761. Guicciardini wrote the Storia d'Italia in 1537 to 1540, and it was first printed in 1561. With this volume, his account of the Italian wars and of Italy's fall from freedom stands whole in English.

The final books gather the harvest of fifty years of invasion and rivalry. Guicciardini ends as he began, a statesman explaining power to anyone wise enough to listen. His work taught Europe a new, analytical way to write history, cool and causal. To finish volume ten is to close one of the founding books of modern historiography.
davis-present-age-inner-life-1853:
Andrew Jackson Davis surveyed the young spiritualist movement in The Present Age and Inner Life, from 1853. Davis, the Poughkeepsie Seer, wrote as the movement's leading thinker. The book follows his earlier Spiritual Intercourse as a sequel. Five years of rappings, circles, and mediums get sorted under his harmonial philosophy.

He defines spiritualism, describes a spiritual congress, and classifies media and their causes. The phenomena of the spiritual spheres receive their own treatment. His system blends Swedenborg, mesmerism, and reform era hope. The first edition captures the movement taking stock of itself. Historians use it to map early spiritualist thought. Davis writes with a prophet's calm certainty.
braid-hypnotic-therapeutics-1853:
Cases fill Braid's Hypnotic Therapeutics, printed in 1853 as a record of hypnotic cures. Braid, the founder of hypnotism, reports patients treated by trance in his practice. Pain, palsy, and nervous ills supply the case histories. Each case states the method, the sittings, and the outcome he observed.

An appendix turns to table moving and spirit rapping, then sweeping the parlors. Braid traces those wonders to unconscious muscular action by the sitters. That reading came decades before the SPR studied the same feats. The appendix is the earliest physiological account of such phenomena. The volume joins clinic and controversy in one binding. Both halves show his method.
zoist-vol-11-1853:
Volume eleven of The Zoist spans April 1853 to January 1854. Elliotson edits on, his journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism in its eleventh year. Case reports of trance cures and painless procedures keep arriving. The somnambulist reports now share an age with table turning and spirit circles.

Mesmerists in these pages claim prior right to the new wonders. Critics answer that trance and fraud explain them all. The thirteen volumes of the run form the movement's archive entire. Volume eleven belongs to its final stretch. The writing stays earnest, detailed, and combative by turns. It records a world of practice that official journals scorned.
plos-pone-0003453:
Penghua Yang and co-authors made drug-producing cattle in this 2008 cloning paper. Their goal was human lactoferrin, a useful milk protein, made at large scale. Older methods of farming such proteins in animals were slow and weak. The team used a new transgenic cloning procedure in cattle.

The cows' mammary glands then served as living bioreactors. Their milk carried functional human lactoferrin. Making medicine in milk could beat factory cell cultures on scale. The paper reports a step toward herds that produce biopharmaceuticals. Large mammal cloning stayed hard and costly, which makes each working drug herd notable for the field.
plos-pone-0003553:
Florian Geier and co-authors modeled plant stem cell control in this 2008 paper. Plants keep pools of flexible stem cells for their whole lives. Those pools sit in meristems, the growing points of shoots and roots. The reference plant Arabidopsis has a well-mapped shoot meristem.

Their quantitative and dynamic model captures how that pool is regulated. It follows signals that balance renewal against differentiation. The equations describe a strategy for never running out of fresh cells. Growers and breeders rely on the same meristem rules. Meristem rules also decide crop size, since flowers and grain start there.
plos-pone-0003653:
François-Denis Desgorces, Geoffroy Berthelot, Nour El Helou, and colleagues published this sports study in PLOS ONE in 2008. They traced best performances in ten famous outdoor events, some dating back to the 1800s. The set runs from the Oxford-Cambridge boat race to the channel swim and beyond.

Across these events, records rose for long stretches and then slowed as they neared bodily limits. The authors argue that the body's own limits, rather than training or will, now set the ceiling. The work maps where human performance in classic endurance events is likely to stall.
plos-pone-0003753:
Cuilin Zhang, Chunfang Qiu, Frank B. Hu, and colleagues published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Vitamin D levels vary widely among pregnant women. The blood marker 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the standard way to gauge them. The team asked whether a mother's level relates to diabetes in pregnancy.

They measured the marker in maternal plasma and compared it with the risk of gestational diabetes mellitus. Their analysis links the mother's vitamin D state to her odds of developing the condition. The finding adds a nutritional thread to the story of blood sugar trouble in pregnancy.
plos-pone-0003853:
Carmen Palacios, Erik Zettler, Ricardo Amils, and colleagues published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The Río Tinto in Spain is an acid river system of natural, ancient origin, unlike acid mine drainage. Microbes from all three domains of life flourish in its extreme waters, with bacteria running most processes.

The team tested rival hypotheses for how such microbial communities assemble. Patchy chemistry along the river let them weigh environment against dispersal. Their reconciling account shows how both forces can shape who lives where in one of Earth's strangest rivers.
plos-pone-0003953:
Michael A. Schillaci, Howard Waitzkin, Tom Sharmen, and co-authors tracked child vaccination in New Mexico in 2008. Shots are a core part of children's primary care. New Mexico is a poor, largely rural state. It has at times struggled to keep childhood immunization rates up.

Their PLOS ONE article evaluated state rates from 1996 to 2006. It focused on shifts in Medicaid enrollment during those years. Medicaid covers many children whose shots public programs track. The study shows how insurance churn can shake a state vaccination program. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004053:
Lu Feng, Peter R. Reeves, Ruiting Lan, and co-authors redated the cholera family tree in 2008. Cholera has erupted from South Asia in seven pandemics. Local outbreaks also struck between the sixth and seventh pandemics. All pandemic strains belong to serotype O1 of Vibrio cholerae.

Their PLOS ONE article recalibrated the molecular clock for those strains. The new timing supports independent origins for the pandemic clones. Separate origins change how the disease's history is told. They also shape guesses about where the next pandemic clone may arise. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004153:
Emily Holmes and colleagues published this proposal paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flashbacks, vivid unwanted memories that feel like reliving the event, are the hallmark symptom of posttraumatic stress disorder. Good treatments exist for the full disorder, but early steps to stop it forming are lacking.

The authors propose a cognitive vaccine: a task done soon after trauma that blocks flashbacks from building up. Their candidate is the computer game Tetris, whose visual demands may compete with the brain's recording of traumatic images. The paper lays out the science behind the idea and how it could be tested as an early aid after trauma.
plos-pone-0004253:
Vincent Paupe and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Friedreich ataxia begins with a shortage of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein, and the shortage kills a subset of neurons. Hallmarks of the disease include low activity of iron-sulfur cluster proteins and a weakened defence against oxidative stress.

The team focused on Nrf2, a master switch of that antioxidant defence. They report that Nrf2 fails to move into the nucleus properly, which undermines the oxidative stress response. A switch stuck outside the control room explains why defences stay off even when they are needed.
plos-pone-0004353:
Anne-Cécile Petit and Jean-François Nicolas published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Understanding how embryos build their structures is a central issue in developmental biology. It is essential for interpreting the massive molecular data now available. In the mouse embryo, watching cell behaviour over the long term is difficult.

The team performed a large-scale clonal analysis, tracing the descendants of single cells in the surface ectoderm. They reveal unexpected complexity in how this outer layer takes shape. Lineage maps like this show the embryo is built by more intricate cell movements than textbooks suggest. Each traced clone is one cell's family story.

frus-1945-50-intel-d153:
A memorandum dated 6 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Staff Committee. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 153 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d253:
Dated 9 December 1947, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the Members of the National Security Council. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 253, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d353:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached Allen W. Dulles on 17 November 1948. Readers meet it as document 353 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles survey team was checking how well the CIA worked, and agencies across Washington were stating their views on the record.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1861-d53:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 June 1861. It is document 53 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams and Seward wrote to each other on the same day more than once that summer. Neither could answer the other's latest word for at least two weeks. Their letters form two lines that cross but never quite meet, a true picture of rule by mail across an ocean. Their crossed letters of June show a bond of trust that distance could not fray. Trust that survives slow mails is the strongest kind a service can build.
frus-1861-d153:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 September 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 153 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing habit of the Paris file appears once more in September. Each man wrote from his own week's facts, not the other's. The record gains from it: two honest views of one bond, neither trimmed to fit the last letter. Neither view was trimmed to please the other, which gives the file its force. Force of that kind is why scholars still read this file with close care.
frus-1861-d253:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands, dated 18 September 1861. Congress received it as Document 253 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d53:
By the date of 26 April 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 53 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d153:
A dispatch of 26 September 1862 from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, as Document 153 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of many Seward letters sent across the Atlantic that fall.

London and Washington were ten days or more apart by mail steamer, so each side often answered news the other had already moved past. That gap shaped the tone of the whole exchange. Short, frequent dispatches like this one kept the envoy supplied with fresh orders and fresh facts as the British cabinet weighed its course. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d253:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 19 February 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 253 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter joined the regular flow between the Department and the Paris legation.

Mid-February 1862 brought the surrender of Fort Donelson, a Union triumph that impressed foreign watchers. Seward could write to Europe from a stronger hand than he had held in months. His letters to Dayton in this season worked that advantage, pressing France to keep its distance from the Confederacy while Union arms advanced. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d353:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to Henri Mercier on 10 January 1862. In a letter printed as Document 353 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier served as the French minister in Washington.

Early January was a settling time after the Trent settlement, with both Britain and France recalculating their American course. French forces were ashore in Mexico, and Washington wanted French aims stated plainly. Seward's letters to Mercier in this season kept the channel warm while harder questions formed behind it. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d453:
Six days after his last order to Vienna, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to John Lothrop Motley on 10 March 1862. The dispatch is Document 453 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The quick follow-up is typical of Seward's style: when news moved, instructions moved with it. That week the ironclads Monitor and Merrimack had just fought in Hampton Roads, an event every naval power in Europe studied closely. Motley needed Washington's account of such events before Vienna's court formed its own. Short orders like this one kept American ministers current, and they make the printed file read like the working log of a government at war.
frus-1862-d553:
The Belgian file opens on 17 March 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Brussels. It is Document 553 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Belgium was a small, industrial kingdom whose king, Leopold I, was uncle and adviser to half the courts of Europe. Sanford, a wealthy and energetic Connecticut man, made Brussels a listening post as much as a legation. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Belgian court. The letter begins a file in which a minor post punches above its weight, because Sanford reported everything and knew everyone.
frus-1862-d653:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to Townsend Harris in Japan on 7 October 1861. Harris was nearing the end of his time as the first American minister there. The letter is document 653 in the Foreign Relations volume covering 1862.

By the fall of 1861 the Civil War filled Seward's desk, yet the Japan file still drew his care. Letters of this kind kept the legation in line with Washington's plans and told Harris what news from home might mean for his work. It is one piece of the steady stream that held a new and fragile link between the two lands.
frus-1863p1-d53:
Stephen R. Mallory wrote to James M. Mason on 30 October 1862. Mallory was the Confederate secretary of the navy; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 53 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mallory wrote to London twice in this file within the week, a sign of how much of his navy was being built in British yards. Mason was his man on the spot, facing the builders and the British law. This letter is part of that traffic. Read against the Adams mail in the same volume, it shows both sides of one fight. One side sought ships for the South. The other drove to stop them.
frus-1863p1-d153:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 10 April 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 153 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a Seward letter often added the point that had just ripened at home. In April 1863 the ripening news was of the war and of Congress's mood. Adams had to know both to speak well in London. This letter is the second half of the day's work from Washington. Filed with its twin, it keeps the exchange's pace into mid-April.
frus-1863p1-d253:
The State Department's mail for London dated 29 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 253 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d353:
A formal note dated 7 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 353 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d453:
Document 453 in the volume is a letter of 9 April 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d553:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 6 June 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d653:
F. W. Seward, the Assistant Secretary of State sent an official note to Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London on 2 November 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
plos-pbio-0020153:
Bing-Hao Luo, Timothy A. Springer, and Junichi Takagi studied how cell anchor proteins grip their targets in PLOS Biology in 2004. Integrins are anchors that let cells hold onto the material around them and onto other cells. Their grip can be weak or strong, and the cell controls that choice.

The authors pinpoint where the two parts of the integrin cross the cell membrane and touch. That contact sets how tightly the outside end holds its ligand. A defined contact site is good news for drug design. Compounds that nudge that contact could loosen the grip of cells in diseases driven by excess adhesion, like clots or cancer spread.
plos-pone-0000153:
Joseph F. Ryan, Maureen E. Mazza, Kevin Pang, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hox genes pattern the body plans of bilaterian animals, from worms to humans, and their cluster was long tied to that group. The authors present evidence from the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, a cnidarian that split off before bilaterians arose.

Their analyses push the origin of the Hox cluster and the Hox code back before bilaterians existed. That challenges the claim that the Hox code is a bilaterian invention. The paper reshapes the story of how the genetic toolkit for building animal bodies first came together.
plos-pone-0000253:
Weronika Fic, François Juge, Johann Soret, and colleagues published this developmental genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the fruit fly, the gene eyeless is a master switch for building an eye. The authors show that eye development is controlled by alternative splicing of eyeless, the cutting and rejoining of its message. That splicing is carried out with the factor SRp55, also called B52.

One gene can thus make different products that steer development differently. The paper maps how splicing choices on a master gene shape a whole organ. The finding adds a layer to the famous eyeless story and to the wider role of splicing in development.
plos-pone-0000353:
Gavin M. Bendle, Shao-An Xue, Angelika Holler, and colleagues published this immunotherapy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. T cells are often tolerant to MDM2, a tumor-associated antigen found on many cancers, because the immune system treats it as self. The authors study that tolerance and report cytokines can restore the T cells' responsiveness to the antigen.

Restored responsiveness comes with a limit, noted in the title: high-avidity T cell function does not come back. The strongest killers stay blunted even when weaker responses revive. That ceiling matters for cancer vaccine design, which must work with the T cells tolerance leaves behind.
plos-pone-0000453:
Tanya Wolff, Jake B. Guinto, and Amy S. Rawls screened fly genes for ones that modify a developmental defect, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The defect involves stbm, a gene needed to orient cells in the eye. In the Drosophila eye, each unit's photoreceptors must both choose their fate and rotate into place.

The screen found modifiers showing that fate and rotation can be genetically uncoupled: one can go wrong while the other stays normal. That separation proves the two steps run on partly independent machinery. Genetic screens of this sort are how biologists take apart a process that looks, from outside, like a single event.
plos-pone-0000553:
Pearl A. Campbell and colleagues mapped where a master stem cell protein touches the genome's control switches, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is Oct4, essential for keeping embryonic stem cells unspecialized. The team found that Oct4 targets regulatory nodes, hub points in the control network, to modulate stem cell function.

A regulator that sits on hubs can retune the whole network with small movements. Mapping those hubs explains how stem cells hold their state and how they might be pushed into other cell types. In 2007, with reprogramming of adult cells newly demonstrated, Oct4's network was among the most studied maps in biology.
plos-pone-0000653:
Russell Garman, Clinton Rubin and Stefan Judex reported that tiny shaking can stir bone-forming cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tissues adapt to mechanical challenges, and the usual explanation runs through deformation of cells or their surrounding matrix. Their result cuts against that assumption. The accelerations they applied were extremely small and came as unconstrained motion.

The title states the outcome: osteoblast activity rose and bone morphology improved, independent of matrix deformation. Osteoblasts are the cells that build bone. If movement signals alone, without strain, can drive them, exercise and device design for bone loss gain a new lever. The finding also reframes how cells sense motion.
plos-pone-0000753:
Marianne A. B. van der Sande, Pauline A. Waight, Maimuna Mendy and colleagues returned to Gambian teenagers vaccinated against hepatitis B as babies. Chronic hepatitis B infection starting in childhood is associated with liver cancer in adult life. Between 1986 and 1990, about 120,000 Gambian newborns joined a randomised trial of infant vaccination, a rare long-term resource.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE report covers two things: long-term protection against chronic carriage in adolescence, and immune responses in a booster trial. If infant vaccination still protects teenagers, booster policy can be set with confidence. Few vaccine questions can be answered over such spans, which makes this cohort precious.
plos-pone-0000853:
Manfred Thiel, Charles C. Caldwell, Simone Kreth and colleagues tested whether removing an oxygen sensor from T cells helps septic mice survive. Sepsis patients may die from an overwhelming systemic immune response, or from immunoparalysis, a later collapse of antibacterial defense. The team hypothesized that T cells activated by bacterial superantigens are prevented from contributing to antibacterial responses in hypoxic, inflamed tissues.

Their title reports that targeted deletion of the HIF-1 alpha gene in T cells prevents that inhibition and improves septic mice survival. HIF-1 alpha is the cell's low-oxygen switch. Releasing T cells from its brake, only in T cells, is a precise immunotherapy idea for sepsis.
plos-pone-0000953:
Alexei Kurakin, Andrzej Swistowski, Susan Wu and colleagues presented the PDZ domain as a system that adapts like a living network, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Proteins link up in specific pairings that wire the cell's interaction networks. PDZ domains, small protein modules that grab the ends of other proteins, are among the best studied of these linkers.

The authors argue for viewing the PDZ domain as a complex adaptive system, one whose behavior emerges from many local rules. That lens changes what counts as an explanation, from a single binding site to a whole pattern of interactions. It is a conceptual paper, aimed at how researchers think about protein networks.
plos-pone-0001053:
Damian Strier and Silvina Ponce Dawson modeled pattern formation inside cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Concentration gradients inside a cell guide division and body patterning. The pair study a model of one enzyme step, run by phosphofructokinase, which is known for producing even oscillations, rhythms in time.

Their model shows that same step can also produce Turing patterns, steady patterns in space named for Alan Turing. Space patterns from a rhythm known step widen the menu of ways cells organize their interiors. The work is mathematical, but its claim is physical: one common reaction can draw both clocks and maps.
plos-pone-0001153:
Sepsis kills by an overwhelming inflammatory response, and a protein called HMGB1 acts as a late driver of that response. Wei Li and co-authors tested a possible rescue in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: a major ingredient of green tea. Bacterial toxins trigger immune cells to release waves of inflammatory signals, first early ones, then late ones such as HMGB1.

The authors report that the green tea ingredient rescued mice from lethal sepsis, partly by inhibiting HMGB1. Because HMGB1 acts late, blocking it could widen the treatment window beyond what early-acting drugs allow. The study is in animals, an early step toward any human use.
plos-pone-0001253:
When a sound and a flash occur together, the brain must judge whether they were simultaneous. Ryota Kanai and colleagues studied how that judgment shifts, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Visual and auditory signals are usually assumed to have fixed processing delays, whose difference sets when the two feel simultaneous.

The authors report dynamic perceptual changes in audiovisual simultaneity, meaning the perceived timing adapts with experience. What counts as simultaneous is recalibrated by recent events. Their findings show that even something as basic as timing perception is plastic, tuned moment by moment.
plos-pone-0001353:
CEA and CEACAM6 are cell adhesion molecules that are up-regulated in roughly 70 percent of human cancers, without structural mutations. Carlos Chan, Pilar Camacho-Leal, and Clifford Stanners tested their effects in transgenic mice, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In vitro systems had shown tumorigenic effects for these molecules, suggesting the correlation with cancer could indicate cause.

The authors report colorectal hyperplasia and dysplasia, overgrowth and abnormal tissue organization, in mice expressing the human CEA family members. That is direct evidence that raising these adhesion proteins can push gut tissue toward precancerous change. The work supports a causal role, not merely a marker's role.
plos-pone-0001453:
Philip Wrage and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on stem like cells taken from fat. Some had claimed these cells come from the same stock that builds nerves. Others claimed a signal called Notch steers their growth and fate. The team tested both claims in mouse cells grown in nerve cell food.

They found the fat cells had only a scant power to act as nerve stem cells. Their nerve like traits were not steered by Notch, nor did they trace to nerve stock. Clear limits like this keep the field honest. They steer clinics away from claims that run ahead of proof.
plos-pone-0001553:
Ana Villar-Garea and Axel Imhof wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on chemical marks on a DNA packing protein in flies. The protein, H1, binds DNA between the spools that wind it. It helps set how open each gene zone is. H1 bears many kinds of marks, but their exact spots were poorly mapped.

The team mapped those marks in fine detail in the fruit fly. Each mark type sat on set sites on the protein. A fine map lets labs test what each mark does to gene use. It adds to the code by which cells tune their genome without changing its letters.
plos-pone-0001653:
Matt Larouche, Uwe Beffert, Joachim Herz, and their co-authors mapped how a signal protein lays out the cerebellum in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The cerebellum, at the back of the brain, is built in neat transverse zones and lengthwise stripes of Purkinje cells. Those adult stripes form when clusters of young Purkinje cells spread out in a set pattern soon after birth, guided by the Reelin signal pathway.

The study examines two Reelin receptors, Apoer2 and Vldlr, and how each shapes the final map. The full text gives the mouse brain images and the stripe patterns when each receptor is missing. It also gives the authors' model of how the two split the work. Faults in this layout can disturb balance and movement, so its rules matter for brain development research.
plos-pone-0001753:
Nicholas Ieronimakis, Gayathri Balasundaram, and Morayma Reyes presented a method to pull pure vessel-lining cells from muscle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Diseases of small vessel endothelium are among the most prevalent illnesses. Yet no method existed to isolate pure endothelial cells from skeletal muscle for study in the lab or in living animals.

Using multicolor fluorescent-activated cell sorting, the team isolated, cultured, and transplanted mouse skeletal muscle endothelial cells. The cells had angiogenic potential, meaning they can form new vessels. The full text gives the sorting recipe and the transplant results. A pure, workable supply of muscle vessel cells opens studies of wound healing, exercise adaptation, and vascular disease.
plos-pone-0001853:
Claudia Lamina, Friedhelm Bongardt, and Helmut Küchenhoff recast a genetics error problem in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Rebuilding haplotypes, the sets of variants inherited together, by statistics from SNP genotypes can misclassify some of them. That is an issue when reading association results or picking subjects with certain types for follow-up studies.

The authors treat phasing error as a classical misclassification problem and introduce sensitivity and specificity as error measures. The full text gives the framework and worked cases. Framing genetic phasing error in the language of clinical testing lets study planners compute plainly how much error their claims can bear.
plos-pone-0001953:
Gul Shad Ali and co-authors filmed two splicing proteins at work inside living cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Splicing is the step that cuts and rejoins gene messages before they are read, and the spliceosome is the machine that does it. Two of its parts, U1-70K and the SR protein family, are key to both standard and variant splicing.

How fast these parts move, and whether they meet inside the cell, was unknown. The team used two glow methods, FRAP and BiFC, to track motion and contact in live cells. Live tracking shows how the splicing machine assembles in real time, not just in crushed extracts.
plos-pone-0002053:
Raffaella Bianucci and co-authors reported the study of a preserved head from before Spanish rule in South America, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The male head was tested with several methods. Hydrogen isotope ratios in hair, which track water and diet, pointed to a South American origin.

Radiocarbon dating by atomic mass spectrometry placed the head in the last pre-Hispanic period, 1418 to 1491 AD, at high probability. The team also read biological rhythms from the hair, which grows in a steady stream and records diet shifts. Work of this kind shows how much history a single specimen can carry.
plos-pone-0002153:
Maya Huguenin, Eliane Müller, Sandra Trachsel-Rösmann, and co-authors studied an enzyme that cuts a key cell glue protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme, meprin beta, is a metal-based protease found in the gut and kidney lining. It had been linked to cancer, but no one knew the steps that connect it to disease.

Using cultured cells that make meprin alpha, meprin beta, or both, the team showed that meprin beta cuts E-cadherin. E-cadherin is the protein that helps lining cells stick to each other, so cutting it weakens the bonds between cells. Looser cell contact is one route by which tumors spread.
plos-pone-0002253:
Mpiko Ntsekhe and co-authors followed heart patients to see how HIV changes one outcome of tuberculosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. TB can infect the sac around the heart. Up to a quarter of those patients later suffer constriction, a stiffening that squeezes the heart, despite anti-TB drugs. Many such patients in Africa also carry HIV.

In this prospective study, patients were watched over time rather than looked back at. The team found that HIV infection went with a lower rate of constriction. A finding like this changes how doctors weigh risks when HIV and TB strike the same heart.
plos-pone-0002353:
Hongjie Li and co-authors found a gene switched on by the fusion protein that defines a rare cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor is a highly aggressive cancer of adolescents and young adults. Its hallmark is a chromosome swap, t(11;22), that fuses the EWS and WT1 genes into one abnormal protein.

The team identifies the adenosine transporter ENT4 as a direct target of that fusion product, and reports ENT4 is highly expressed in this tumor. A direct target of the driving fusion is both a marker of the disease and a candidate point of attack for future drugs.
plos-pone-0002453:
Surcel and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Alexandra Surcel, Douglas Koshland, Hong Ma, among others. Its subject is cohesin Interaction with Centromeric Minichromosomes Shows a Multi-Complex Rod-Shaped Structure. Cohesin is the protein complex responsible for maintaining sister chromatid cohesion.

Cohesin interacts with centromeres and specific loci along chromosome arms known as Chromosome Attachment Regions (CARs). The cohesin holocomplex contains four subunits. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002553:
Xu, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Jun Xu, Xinxian Deng, Christine M. Disteche, among others. Its subject is sex-Specific Expression of the X-Linked Histone Demethylase Gene Jarid1c in Brain. Jarid1c, an X-linked gene coding for a histone demethylase, plays an important role in brain development and function.

Notably, JARID1C mutations cause mental retardation and increased aggression in humans. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002653:
In 2008, Seema Husain and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about variants of ST8SIA1 are associated with risk of developing multiple sclerosis. The catalog record names Seema Husain first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system of unknown etiology with both genetic and environmental factors playing a. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002753:
In 2008, Cyrille Hoarau and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was supernatant from bifidobacterium differentially modulates transduction signaling pathways for biological functions of human dendritic cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Cyrille Hoarau and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Probiotic bacteria have been shown to modulate immune responses and could have therapeutic effects in allergic and inflammatory disorders. A further point appears in the abstract. However, the signaling pathways engaged by probiotics are poorly understood. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002853:
In 2008, Johnathon R. Walls and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about Three-Dimensional analysis of vascular development in the mouse embryo. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Johnathon R. Walls, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Key vasculogenic ( de-novo vessel forming) and angiogenic (vessel remodelling) events occur in the mouse embryo between embryonic days (E) 8.0 and 10.0 of. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002953:
María Sáez, José González-Sánchez, Reposo Ramírez-Lorca and co-authors tested the CAPN10 gene in a Spanish sample in 2008. Heart and vessel disease is the top cause of illness and death in the industrialized world. Risk factors cluster in families, but the genetic part was still poorly understood.

CAPN10, which codes for calpain 10, had been linked to diabetes traits before. The study checks its link to insulin resistance phenotypes, the traits that show insulin working poorly. Published in PLOS ONE, it adds population data from Spain to a debated gene story. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003053:
Soline Lacour, Emmanuelle Bechet, Alain Cozzone and co-authors studied a bacterial kinase crossroads in E. coli in 2008. A new class of bacterial enzymes called BY-kinases adds phosphate to tyrosine, much as eukaryotic kinases do, yet they share no structure with them. Only a few of their targets were known.

One target is UDP-glucose dehydrogenase, an enzyme tied to making colanic acid, a protective coating. Its phosphorylation sits at the crossroads of coating synthesis and polymyxin resistance, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, that junction links surface building to antibiotic defense in one step.
plos-pone-0003153:
Didem Göz, Keith Studholme, Douglas A. Lappi and colleagues test how light sets the body clock in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some responses to light do not form images. One is the syncing of daily rhythms to day and night. These responses use the classic rods and cones.
